summary: Applies the IPv6 over NBMA architecture to ATM networks. It allows normal host behavior for neighbor discovery while also permitting shortcut ATM connections. It is a proposed standard and was updated by RFC 8064.

eli5.summary: ATM was a network type that makes direct connections. This explains how new internet addresses work on it, and how to make quick shortcuts.

questions: how is ipv6 carried over atm
what is the default mtu for ipv6 over atm
what is null encapsulation in ipv6 over atm
how are ipv6 interface tokens built on atm
subtitle: The ATM-specific details for carrying IPv6 packets over permanent and switched ATM circuits.

tldr.problem: IPv6 needs concrete rules for each kind of link. ATM links are connection-oriented and have no broadcast, so the general IPv6 over NBMA architecture needs ATM-specific code points.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC fixes the AAL5 and LLC/SNAP encapsulation, the default MTU of 9180 bytes, the encoding of the Neighbor Discovery link-layer address option, and several ways to build interface tokens, for both PVC and SVC modes.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard and was updated by RFC 8064. A minimal IPv6/ATM driver only has to support PVC mode.

today: RFC 2492 is a Proposed Standard and was updated by RFC 8064. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Scope and Companion Document
sections.content:
RFC 2492 is the ATM-specific companion to the working group's architecture document, RFC 2491, which describes IPv6 over Non Broadcast Multiple Access (NBMA) networks. Terminology and architecture are not repeated here. Only the ATM details are given.

The RFC covers two kinds of ATM service: point to point PVCs (permanent virtual circuits), and flexible point to point and point to multipoint SVCs (switched virtual circuits). The design lets hosts run Neighbor Discovery in the conventional way and also allows 'shortcut' ATM forwarding paths when SVCs are used.

A minimally conforming IPv6/ATM driver SHALL support PVC mode. A driver that supports full SVC mode SHALL also support PVC mode.
sections.eli5: This note only covers the ATM part of a bigger plan. Computers can use fixed phone-line style links, or links they dial up when needed. The simple fixed kind must always work.

sections.title: PVC Mode
sections.content:
In PVC mode each PVC connects exactly two nodes, so an IPv6/ATM interface has only one neighbor on the link. MARS and NHRP are not necessary, because multicast and broadcast collapse into an ATM-level unicast. Dynamically discovered shortcuts are not supported.

PVC links do not use link-layer addresses, so the link-layer address options SHOULD NOT be included in Neighbor Discovery messages. If one is present, it SHOULD be ignored. The RFC neither requires nor forbids extensions to Neighbor Discovery for PVCs, such as Inverse Neighbor Discovery.

The default MTU on a PVC link is 9180 bytes, as specified in RFC 1626, and other values MAY be used. Interface tokens need only be unique between the two nodes on the PVC.
sections.eli5: A fixed link has just two ends, like two tin cans on a string. Nobody needs to ask who is at the other end, so no address lookup is needed.

sections.title: Encapsulation of IPv6 Packets
sections.content:
Following the model in RFC 1483, AAL5 is the default adaptation layer and LLC/SNAP is the default encapsulation. This holds for unicast and multicast packets on both PVC and SVC links. The default unicast encapsulation is an LLC of 0xAA-AA-03, an OUI of 0x00-00-00, a PID of 0x86-DD, and then the IPv6 packet.

On SVCs, multicast packets use the MARS encapsulation: LLC 0xAA-AA-03, OUI 0x00-00-5E, PID 0x00-01, then a two-octet pkt$cmi field, then 0x86DD and the IPv6 packet. The driver's Cluster Member ID SHALL be copied into pkt$cmi before transmission.

Drivers MAY support null encapsulation as a configurable option, where the IPv6 packet goes straight to AAL5. Both ends MUST be configured for it (on PVCs) or agree during call SETUP (on SVCs), and the circuit cannot then carry other protocols. On SVCs it SHALL NOT be used between the driver and its local MARS, and its use is not encouraged with MARS/NHRP/ND. PPP over AAL5 PVCs is not covered.
sections.eli5: Every IPv6 packet goes into an envelope with a small label saying what is inside. You can skip the label if the line only ever carries IPv6, but then both ends must agree.

sections.title: Control Messages and the Link-Layer Address Option
sections.content:
MARS control messages keep the encapsulation from RFC 2022 (LLC 0xAA-AA-03, OUI 0x00-00-5E, PID 0x00-03), and NHRP control messages keep the one from RFC 2332. In both, the address family field stays 0x0F (ATM addresses) and the protocol field SHALL be 0x86DD (IPv6). Protocol address length fields are either 0 or 16, the full IPv6 address.

The Neighbor Discovery link-layer address option carries an NTL octet, which gives the type and length of the ATM number, and an STL octet for the subaddress. In NTL the top bit is reserved and MUST be zero. The next bit says whether the number is in ATM Forum AESA format (0) or native E.164 format (1), and the bottom 6 bits give the length in octets.

If there is no subaddress, the STL octet MUST be zero. A subaddress is always in AESA format. The NBMA Number is always present, and the NBMA Subaddress may be absent. Octet order is the same as in MARS and NHRP messages.
sections.eli5: The address tag says how long the ATM address is and what style it is written in. A second tag does the same for an optional extra address.

sections.title: SVC Signalling and MTU
sections.content:
When an IPv6 node places a call to another, it SHOULD follow the procedures in RFC 1755 and RFC 1626 for signalling UNI 3.0/3.1 SVCs and negotiating the MTU. The default IP MTU is 9180 bytes.

IPv6 Path MTU Discovery (RFC 1981) is used instead of the IPv4 mechanism. IPv6 nodes are not required to implement it, but IPv6/ATM nodes SHOULD. Since each VC negotiates an MTU, a Packet Too Big message should never be triggered between two directly connected nodes. When nodes communicate through routers, Path MTU Discovery works as on legacy networks.
sections.eli5: Before talking, the two computers agree how big a packet can be. If they both do that, nothing should ever be too big for the line.

sections.title: Interface Tokens
sections.content:
For both modes, one of several methods SHALL be used to build the interface token (the low part of an IPv6 address, as in RFC 2373).

  • ESI based: if the interface has an AESA, the token MAY be [0x00][ESI][SEL]: a zero octet, the six-octet ESI and the one-octet SEL. The Global/Local bit is cleared, so the token is not globally unique.
  • 48-bit MAC based: if the NIC has a unique 48-bit value, the token MAY be built from it as in RFC 2373.
  • EUI-64 based: if the NIC has a unique EUI-64, the interface SHOULD use it, with only the Global/Local bit inverted.
  • Native E.164 based: the E.164 digits MAY be packed two to an octet, with the lower four bits of the first octet set to 0.
  • No identifier: the method in Appendix A of RFC 2373 SHALL be used.

Several logical interfaces on one port are told apart by their ESI and SEL combination. Virtual hosts MUST NOT end up advertising the same interface token on the same link, which can be achieved with different SEL values, ESI values, or both.
sections.eli5: Each computer needs a unique name tag for its network card. It can build one from the serial number printed on the card, or from its phone-style number, and two helpers sharing a card must never pick the same tag.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC introduces no new security mechanisms. It states that all current IPv6 security mechanisms work without modification over ATM, including authentication and encryption for both the Neighbor Discovery protocols and the exchange of IPv6 data packets.
sections.eli5: Nothing new is added for safety. The locks already used for IPv6 work just the same on ATM.
